titleText.es: Los foros de huracanes están llenos de comentarios excitados sobre la presión central y la velocidad del viento y comparaciones con Camille y 1931 y 1938, con la coletilla de rigor sobre lo trágico que sería que muriera alguien y que esperan que no sea para tanto.
titleText.en: Hurricane forums are full of excited comments about central pressure and wind speed and comparisons to Camille and 1931 and 1938, with hastily-tacked-on notes about how it will be tragic if anyone dies and they hope it's a dud.
titleText.noteEn: The English text is the official xkcd title text. The Spanish raster translates intern as residente and preserves the archive wording DISPARARLE even though its following target, SUS VENTANAS, is plural; that number mismatch is explained only at the occurrence. Vision also split ATRACCIÓN, ESPERANZAS, and ATERRORIZADOS across printed line breaks, lost the accents in HARÁN, ÓRGANOS, and SOLÍAN, and misread HUMANOS and CONVERSACIONES. This artifact follows the visible raster exactly.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I root for; I cheer on
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Animo is the present form of animar for the speaker. It has no written accent; ánimo with an accent is a noun or an encouraging exclamation.

example.es: Animo a mi equipo desde casa.
example.en: I cheer on my team from home.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Noticias is grammatically plural in Spanish even when English uses the singular mass noun news.

example.es: Veo las noticias por la mañana.
example.en: I watch the news in the morning.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: of; no separate word before a hoped-for event
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Esperanza normally uses de before a noun and de que before a full statement about what is hoped for.

example.es: Tengo la esperanza de que vuelva.
example.en: I hope that she returns.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they will become (as part of se harán)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Harán is hacer's future form for more than one subject. With se and a description, hacerse means to become; hacer uses the irregular future stem har-.

example.es: Los días se harán más largos.
example.en: The days will become longer.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they will devastate; they will sweep through
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Arrasar can mean destroying or devastating a place as something moves through it.

example.en: The flames will devastate the forest.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Afectan is the present form used with a plural subject.

example.en: The changes affect the schedule.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: After sentirse, mal can describe feeling physically unwell or emotionally bad about something.

example.es: Me siento mal por el error.
example.en: I feel bad about the mistake.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Na is a very informal dismissive response. Nah is another common spelling; this comic prints na.

example.en: Nah, I'd rather stay here.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Natural has the same form with masculine and feminine singular nouns.

example.en: It is a natural reaction.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses por after atracción or sentir atracción to introduce the object of attraction, where English often uses to.

example.en: She feels an attraction to the sea.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: A transbordador transports people or cargo between points; transbordador espacial is a space shuttle.

example.es: El transbordador lleva pasajeros a la isla.
example.en: The shuttle carries passengers to the island.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Espacial can also mean spatial in other contexts. After transbordador, it identifies a space shuttle.

example.en: They study space exploration.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to miss; to miss out on
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With a matching me, te, or se marker, perderse algo means failing to experience an event or opportunity. With two verbs, that marker may appear before the first conjugated verb: no te quieres perder.

example.en: I don't want to miss the movie.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Vestirte joins the unchanged verb vestir, to dress, with te, which identifies one familiar listener as the person being dressed.

example.en: You can get dressed here.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Colarte joins colar with te. In the pronominal verb colarse, it means entering somewhere secretly or without permission.

example.es: No debes colarte en la fiesta.
example.en: You should not sneak into the party.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: into; required after colarse before a place
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Use en after colarse to introduce the place entered secretly.

example.en: He sneaked into the building.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: A sala de operaciones is an operating room used for surgery.

example.es: El hospital tiene dos salas de operaciones.
example.en: The hospital has two operating rooms.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por si, 'in case'
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Por combines with unaccented si before a possible event to form por si.

example.es: Lleva agua por si hace calor.
example.en: Take water in case it is hot.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por si, 'in case'
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Si remains unaccented in por si and introduces the uncertain event for which someone prepares.

example.es: Cierra la ventana por si llueve.
example.en: Close the window in case it rains.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Paciente has the same written form for a male or female patient.

example.en: The patient is waiting for the doctor.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cosechar literally means gathering a crop and can extend to harvesting organs in medical language.

example.en: They harvest the grapes in September.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Señal can be a physical sign that directs road users, not only a signal or indication.

example.en: Follow the road signs.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dirigir can mean sending movement or traffic toward a destination.

example.es: Van a dirigir el tráfico hacia el puente.
example.en: They are going to direct traffic toward the bridge.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de mala muerte
cardDefinitions.noteEn: De is fixed inside de mala muerte, a description meaning seedy, shabby, or disreputable.

example.es: Entraron en un bar de mala muerte.
example.en: They entered a seedy bar.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Mala is part of the fixed expression de mala muerte rather than an ordinary adjective agreeing with the preceding noun.

example.es: Es un hotel de mala muerte.
example.en: It is a seedy hotel.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; completes de mala muerte
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The full expression de mala muerte describes something as shabby or disreputable; it is not a literal reference to death.

example.es: Trabaja en un local de mala muerte.
example.en: He works in a shabby establishment.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Plagadas agrees with a feminine plural noun and is followed by de before what fills or overruns it.

example.es: Las calles están plagadas de baches.
example.en: The streets are riddled with potholes.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Plagado de introduces what something is filled, covered, or overrun with.

example.es: El texto está plagado de errores.
example.en: The text is riddled with errors.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Abrojo can also name a thorny burr. On a road here, the plural refers to sharp obstacles placed to puncture tires.

example.en: The caltrops punctured the tires.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Reventar describes something bursting; with tires, English commonly says blow out.

example.es: Los globos revientan con el calor.
example.en: The balloons burst in the heat.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Empiezas is empezar's present form for one familiar listener.

example.en: You start working tomorrow.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to shoot at him, her, or it
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dispararle joins disparar with singular le, which marks one target. Use dispararles when that target is plural; a following phrase beginning with a can name the target explicitly.

example.en: You must not shoot at the animal.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: at; introduces the target after disparar
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After disparar, a can introduce the person or thing aimed at.

example.en: They shot at the target.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Huyen is huir's present form for a plural subject.

example.en: The animals flee from the fire.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: them; marks several targets of dar caza
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In dar caza a alguien, le or les can stand before dar for the person or people being pursued.

example.en: The guards hunt them down.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; supplies the verb in dar caza, 'to hunt down'
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Das is dar's present form for one familiar listener. In dar caza, dar is not translated literally as give.

example.en: You hunt down the fugitive.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; completes dar caza, 'to hunt down'
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Caza means hunting by itself, but dar caza works as a fixed expression for pursuing and catching a target.

example.es: La policía da caza al ladrón.
example.en: The police hunt down the thief.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a caballo, 'on horseback'
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The fixed expression uses a before caballo without an article.

example.en: We travel on horseback.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they used to; they would usually
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Solían is soler's imperfect-past form for more than one person. It is followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: They used to walk together.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: realized; noticed (as part of me di cuenta)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Di is dar's completed-past form for the speaker. With me and cuenta, it forms me di cuenta, not the literal meaning gave.

example.en: I noticed the mistake.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Manteniendo is mantener's ongoing-action form. With conversación, mantener can mean having, carrying on, or keeping a conversation going rather than physically maintaining something.

example.en: We are having a calm conversation.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone feels bad, unwell, or guilty?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker with a form of sentir, followed by mal.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The short marker and sentir change with the person: me siento, te sientes, se siente, and nos sentimos. Mal stays unchanged and can describe physical illness or an unpleasant or guilty feeling.

example.es: Ana se siente mal por el comentario.
example.en: Ana feels bad about the comment.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone sneaks into a place?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker with a form of colar, then en and the place.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form is colarse. In present-time forms, its o often changes to ue: ella se cuela. En introduces the place entered secretly or without permission.

example.es: Ella se cuela en la fiesta.
example.en: She sneaks into the party.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say 'in case' before a possible event?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use por si, then an ordinary present-time verb form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Si has no accent here. Even when the possible event lies in the future, Spanish normally uses a present-time form after por si: por si llueve, not a future form. The main clause names the precaution.

example.es: Lleva un abrigo por si hace frío.
example.en: Take a coat in case it is cold.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you describe a place or thing as seedy, shabby, or disreputable?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put de mala muerte after the noun.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is a fixed description, not a literal reference to death. Its wording stays de mala muerte even after a masculine or plural noun.

example.es: Dormimos en un hotel de mala muerte.
example.en: We slept in a seedy hotel.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is riddled with or overrun by something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of plagado that matches the described noun, then de and what fills it.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A noun is a naming word such as informe or calles. Plagado changes to plagada, plagados, or plagadas to match that noun; de stays unchanged before what is present in an unwanted abundance.

example.es: El informe está plagado de errores.
example.en: The report is riddled with errors.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone hunts down or pursues a target?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of dar followed by caza, then a and the target; a target already known can instead be represented by le or les before dar.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Only dar changes for the person and time: doy caza, das caza, dan caza. Caza stays fixed. Al is the required combination of a and el, as in dar caza al fugitivo; le is singular and les is plural when those short target words are used.

example.es: La policía da caza al fugitivo.
example.en: The police hunt down the fugitive.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone travels or does something on horseback?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a caballo after the action.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A caballo is a fixed manner expression. The a has no separate English word here, caballo stays singular, and Spanish does not put an article between them.

example.en: They arrived on horseback.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that people have or carry on a conversation?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of mantener with conversación, or conversaciones for more than one.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Mantener literally often means to keep or maintain, but with conversación it describes having or carrying on the exchange. Mantener changes with the person and time; for example, yo mantengo and estamos manteniendo.

example.en: We have a calm conversation.

applications.exampleEs: ME HE DADO CUENTA DE QUE
applications.explanationEn: Me matches the speaker; he dado supplies the completed form of dar; cuenta completes the fixed expression; and de que introduces the fact noticed.
He is the present form of haber for the speaker, and dado is dar's completed-action form.
Secreta is the feminine singular form of secreto; adding -mente forms secretamente, which describes how the speaker roots for the hurricanes.
A marks the personified hurricanes as the direct target of animo, and los huracanes completes the plural target phrase.
Se with harán forms hacerse for a plural subject, and enormes names the resulting state.
Harán uses hacer's irregular future stem har- plus the plural ending -án.
Arrasarán keeps the full form arrasar and adds the plural future ending -án.
Los replaces the masculine plural things affected and stands directly before the conjugated verb afectan.
The two words form the fixed contrast marker en realidad.
Me matches the speaker, siento is the corresponding form of sentir, and mal supplies the negative feeling.

applications.explanationEn: Hace comes before un rato to place the later realization a short while in the past.
Here que connects the elapsed-time phrase to the event it dates; natural English usually restructures the wording rather than translating que alone.
Me matches the speaker, di supplies the completed-past form of dar, cuenta completes the expression, and de que introduces the fact noticed.
Di uses the preterite because it presents the realization as one completed event in the past.
Estamos matches we, and manteniendo supplies the ongoing action with its -iendo ending.
Manteniendo is the ongoing form of mantener, and conversaciones is the plural exchange being carried on.
Completa takes -mente to form completamente, which intensifies how different the conversations are.
